article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Hybrid
Genetics: Jealousy × Baker’s Dozen
Breeder: Exotic Genetix
THC Content: 20–26%
CBD Content: 1%
Terpene Profile: Caryophyllene , Limonene , Myrcene
Primary Flavors: Sweet vanilla, creamy gelato, sugary berries
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–10 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: October
Indoor Yield: Moderate to High
Outdoor Yield: Variable
Grow Difficulty: Intermediate

Royalty arrives with a genetic pedigree that reads like a collection of modern cannabis breeding achievements. Jealousy, one of the most influential descendants of Gelato , meets Baker’s Dozen, a resin-heavy hybrid built around the creamy sweetness of Cookies genetics and the colorful complexity of Rainbow Chip . The combination produces a marijuana cultivar with considerable potential for visual appeal, aromatic richness, and potent psychoactive effects. Its fragrance draws from sweet vanilla, ripe fruit, peppery herbs, and the distinctive earthy gas associated with contemporary California hybrids.

Developed by Exotic Genetix as part of the Baker’s Dozen Reloaded collection, Royalty represents a deliberate effort to unite two established genetic families without losing their individual characteristics. The resulting cannabis plants can develop dense, crystalline flowers with contrasting green and purple pigmentation, while their effects may progress from mental euphoria toward substantial physical relaxation. For enthusiasts interested in the continuing evolution of Cookies and Gelato genetics, this cultivar offers a particularly intriguing combination of heritage, flavor, and modern breeding potential.
Genetics and Lineage

Royalty originated from a cross between Jealousy and Baker’s Dozen, bringing together two influential branches of contemporary American cannabis genetics. Exotic Genetix selected Jealousy as the female parent, using a reversed Baker’s Dozen selection to produce feminized offspring. Jealousy was originally created by Seed Junky Genetics through the combination of Gelato #41 and Sherbet BX1. Gelato #41 descends from Sunset Sherbet and Thin Mint Girl Scout Cookies , contributing dense flowers, substantial resin production, and creamy dessert-like aromas. Sherbet BX1 represents a backcrossed Sunset Sherbet breeding line, reinforcing characteristics associated with sweet fruit, earthy spice, and aromatic complexity. This repeated Sherbet influence gives Jealousy a particularly concentrated genetic identity within the larger Cookies family .

Baker’s Dozen introduces additional layers of American hybrid breeding through its parents, Milk & Cookies and Rainbow Chip. Milk & Cookies combines Cookies & Cream with Triple OG, bringing together vanilla-like sweetness and the deeper characteristics of classic OG Kush genetics. Cookies & Cream itself originated from Girl Scout Cookies and Starfighter F2, introducing additional resin production and dense flower development. Triple OG contributes influences associated with Triangle Kush , Constantine, and Master Yoda, reinforcing earthy pungency and physically relaxing characteristics. Rainbow Chip supplies a different aromatic personality through Sunset Sherbet and Mint Chocolate Chip , introducing fruit sweetness, herbal mint, chocolate-like richness, and colorful flower potential.

The relationship between these genetic families is particularly important. Sunset Sherbet appears within both sides of Royalty’s ancestry, while Girl Scout Cookies genetics are represented through several different breeding pathways. This overlapping heritage creates opportunities for familiar characteristics to reappear in new combinations, including creamy sweetness, dense flowers, and pungent aromatic resin. Exotic Genetix released Royalty in feminized photoperiod seed form as part of the second batch of its Baker’s Dozen Reloaded collection. Rather than introducing an unrelated genetic influence, the breeder concentrated several successful Cookies-era lineages into a new hybrid capable of expressing characteristics from Jealousy and Baker’s Dozen.
Effects and Experience

The psychoactive experience associated with Royalty may begin with a noticeable cerebral uplift, reflecting the engaging character of its Jealousy ancestry. A change in mood can accompany the initial effects, while music, conversation, and familiar recreational activities may become more absorbing. Some consumers may experience mild euphoria, increased sociability, or a greater appreciation for sensory details. Jealousy contributes a reputation for balanced mental and physical effects, creating the potential for an experience that feels engaging without becoming immediately overwhelming. However, the precise effects of Royalty have not been standardized through controlled studies, and cannabinoid concentration, dosage, and individual tolerance remain important variables.

Physical relaxation may become increasingly apparent as intoxication develops. The substantial Sherbet, Cookies, and OG influences create the potential for reduced restlessness, heavier bodily sensations, and a gradual transition toward a calmer state. At moderate amounts, experienced consumers may remain comfortable enjoying leisurely activities, while larger doses can produce fatigue, impaired concentration, and sleepiness. Its advertised THC potential of approximately 20–26% makes substantial intoxication possible, particularly among individuals with limited tolerance. Excessive consumption may cause dry mouth, dizziness, anxiety, increased heart rate, or uncomfortable changes in thought patterns. Regardless of whether the experience feels uplifting or relaxing, cannabis can impair coordination, judgment, and reaction time.
Medical Benefits

Royalty’s potential combination of cerebral uplift and physical relaxation may interest medical marijuana patients exploring cannabinoid-based approaches to persistent discomfort. THC interacts with the body’s endocannabinoid system, influencing neurological pathways involved in pain perception, appetite regulation, and other physiological functions. Clinical research suggests that certain cannabinoid preparations may provide modest benefits for selected chronic pain conditions, although effectiveness varies considerably. The cultivar’s potentially calming physical character may appeal to individuals who prefer a less immediately sedating experience. Nevertheless, no clinical trials have established Royalty itself as an effective treatment for chronic pain, muscle spasms, or another specific medical condition.

Sleep difficulties, appetite changes, and stress-related discomfort represent additional reasons some consumers consider THC-dominant marijuana. Temporary changes in mood may encourage relaxation, while larger amounts can produce drowsiness or increased hunger. These potential effects must be balanced against the risks associated with frequent high-potency weed consumption. Repeated use can contribute to tolerance, dependence, impaired memory, and changes in normal sleep patterns. THC may also worsen anxiety or provoke uncomfortable psychological reactions in susceptible individuals. Patients managing cardiovascular or psychiatric conditions, or taking prescription medications, should consult a qualified healthcare professional before consuming cannabis. Product-specific laboratory testing and individual medical circumstances remain essential when evaluating potential medical applications.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Royalty’s expected aromatic personality reflects the concentration of sweet dessert genetics within its family tree. Jealousy contributes characteristics associated with creamy gelato, earthy spice, and subtle fruit sweetness, while Baker’s Dozen introduces richer vanilla, cookie dough, and bakery-like qualities. Mature flowers may produce a fragrance resembling sweet cream layered over ripe berries and citrus peel, followed by a sharper impression of pungent gas. The interaction between these contrasting aromas creates the potential for considerable sensory complexity. Some phenotypes may emphasize creamy sweetness and floral undertones, while others could develop more pronounced earthy, peppery, or fuel-like characteristics. Breaking apart resinous flowers can intensify these aromatic layers as volatile compounds are released.

Several terpenes commonly encountered in the parental families may contribute to the finished profile. Beta-caryophyllene introduces peppery warmth and woody depth, while limonene provides citrus-associated brightness. Myrcene can reinforce earthy and herbal characteristics, and linalool may introduce subtle floral softness when present. Their actual concentrations in Royalty require laboratory analysis, since no standardized terpene ranking has been established across the genetic population. The recognizable vanilla, cookie, and berry impressions also depend on combinations of volatile aromatic compounds beyond conventional terpene classifications. On the palate, sweeter phenotypes may emphasize creamy gelato and vanilla before developing into earthy spice and pungent fuel. Proper drying, curing, and storage help preserve the delicate compounds responsible for these contrasting flavors.
Growing Information

Royalty combines the dense flowering characteristics associated with Jealousy and the productive resin development of Baker’s Dozen. Plants may display compact-to-medium structures with sturdy branches and relatively closely spaced flowering sites, although individual phenotypes can differ considerably. Its parental genetics are associated with substantial trichome coverage, giving the finished flowers the potential for a heavily frosted appearance. Mature buds may develop combinations of forest-green and purple pigmentation, with bright orange pistils contrasting against pale resin glands. The degree of coloration depends on inherited characteristics and environmental conditions rather than cannabinoid potency. Some selections may remain relatively compact, while others develop more substantial lateral branching and flowering stretch.

Indoor flowering is expected to require approximately eight to ten weeks, based on the maturation characteristics of the parental lines and early cultivation observations. Individual selections may finish closer to nine weeks, although the breeder has not established a universal flowering duration for every phenotype. The plant’s potentially compact structure makes even canopy development important, particularly when multiple flowering branches compete for light. Dense buds may benefit from additional structural support as they gain weight, while adequate ventilation helps reduce moisture accumulation within crowded flowering sites. The cultivar’s resin potential also makes careful environmental management important during late flowering. Published indoor yield figures have not been standardized, so production should be evaluated according to the individual plant rather than assumptions based on its parent strains.

Outdoor cultivation may be possible in regions with sufficient sunlight and relatively dry autumn conditions. October provides a preliminary Northern Hemisphere harvest expectation, although actual maturation depends on local climate, seasonal daylight changes, and phenotype. Plants given adequate space may develop broader branching structures than those maintained indoors, potentially supporting substantial flower production. Dense buds require protection from prolonged rainfall and excessive humidity because moisture retention can encourage fungal contamination. Careful postharvest drying and curing are particularly valuable for preserving the cultivar’s creamy dessert aromas and pungent undertones. Intermediate cultivation experience is beneficial for managing phenotype variation, maintaining airflow, and protecting the resin-rich flowers that characterize this genetic family.
FAQ
Is Royalty indica or sativa?

Royalty is a hybrid created by crossing Jealousy with Baker’s Dozen. Its genetic background combines several influential Cookies, Gelato, and Sherbet breeding lines. Although some descriptions emphasize indica-associated relaxation, a precise indica-to-sativa percentage has not been established for the original Exotic Genetix release. Its psychoactive effects depend on cannabinoid concentration, consumption amount, and individual tolerance rather than genetic classification alone.
How much THC does Royalty have?

Published seed descriptions identify THC potential of approximately 20–26%. These concentrations represent advertised expectations rather than guaranteed results for every phenotype. Individual plants may produce different cannabinoid profiles depending on genetics, growing conditions, and harvest maturity. CBD concentrations are generally expected to remain low, making Royalty predominantly a THC-focused marijuana cultivar.
What does Royalty taste like?

The genetic background suggests a combination of sweet vanilla, creamy gelato, ripe berries, citrus, cookie dough, and earthy spice. Jealousy contributes pungent dessert-related characteristics, while Baker’s Dozen introduces additional bakery sweetness and aromatic depth. Some phenotypes may express stronger fuel or peppery notes, creating contrast with the creamier flavors.
How long does Royalty take to flower?

Indoor flowering is expected to require approximately eight to ten weeks, with some early cultivation observations indicating maturity around 63 days. The cultivar is photoperiod-dependent rather than autoflowering. Individual phenotypes may differ in flowering stretch, bud density, and final maturation time. Outdoor harvest timing has not been standardized by the breeder.
Who bred Royalty, and what are its parent strains?

Royalty was developed by Exotic Genetix using Jealousy as the female parent and a reversed Baker’s Dozen selection. Jealousy was originally created by Seed Junky Genetics from Gelato #41 and Sherbet BX1. Baker’s Dozen combines Milk & Cookies with Rainbow Chip. The resulting cultivar was released as feminized photoperiod seeds within the Baker’s Dozen Reloaded collection.
Final Thoughts on Royalty

Royalty represents a concentrated expression of contemporary Cookies and Sherbet breeding, combining several influential genetic families within one carefully constructed hybrid. Exotic Genetix united the creamy, pungent character of Jealousy with the productive, dessert-oriented genetics of Baker’s Dozen, creating a marijuana strain with substantial potential for aromatic complexity and visually impressive flowers. The repeated Sunset Sherbet and Girl Scout Cookies influences help explain its expected combination of vanilla sweetness, earthy spice, and dense resin production. Its place within the Baker’s Dozen Reloaded collection also reflects the continuing importance of established parental lines in modern American cannabis breeding.

For experienced cannabis enthusiasts, the cultivar offers an opportunity to explore a new expression of Jealousy and its relationship with the broader Cookies family. Growers may appreciate its potential for compact, heavily frosted flowers and relatively manageable flowering requirements, particularly when phenotype selection and flower quality are priorities. Although individual cannabinoid and terpene concentrations require laboratory confirmation, the breeder’s documented lineage establishes a clear genetic identity. Royalty ultimately demonstrates how familiar cannabis families can produce fresh combinations of sensory and horticultural characteristics, preserving the influence of Gelato, Sherbet, and Cookies genetics within a distinctive modern weed hybrid.
